note.text: Internal value is purchasing power over goods and services. For a fixed amount of money, a higher comparable price level means less purchasing power. A price index compares the cost of the same defined basket with its base cost. A purchasing-power index relative to the same base is the reciprocal price ratio scaled to the base. External value concerns exchange against another currency; it is not the same measurement. These exercises use invented baskets and no current exchange rate.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to distinguish internal purchasing power from external exchange value and calculate a reciprocal index. Builds on: money stock, transactions and comparable units. Leads to: basket practical and inflation measurement.

sections.heading: Understand the economics
sections.text: Internal value is purchasing power over goods and services. For a fixed amount of money, a higher comparable price level means less purchasing power. A price index compares the cost of the same defined basket with its base cost. A purchasing-power index relative to the same base is the reciprocal price ratio scaled to the base. External value concerns exchange against another currency; it is not the same measurement. These exercises use invented baskets and no current exchange rate.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: Original basket: base cost {2000} CFA francs; later cost {2500}. The price index is {100*2500/2000}. The purchasing-power index of a fixed unit is {100*2000/2500}. The higher price index does not mean the fixed balance buys more. This basket is a teaching model, not a national consumer-price series.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Keep basket composition fixed and label which index is requested. Divide later by base for prices and base by later for purchasing power, then scale. Do not confuse an index level with a percentage change or infer an exchange rate from an internal price index.
